title: Social Stratification and Structural Function
text:
Social stratification refers to a society's categorization of its people into rankings based on factors such as wealth, income, race, and education. These hierarchical structures are not random; they create divisions that profoundly influence life opportunities and resource distribution across generations.

Functionalist perspectives argue that social inequality is necessary and beneficial because differences in talent lead to differing levels of required training and compensation. In this view, the most critical roles within a society naturally receive greater rewards to incentivize individuals to fill them effectively.

Conversely, conflict theory posits that stratification systems primarily serve to maintain power among dominant groups. This perspective suggests that the existing hierarchy is not meritocratic but rather an institutionalized mechanism of control that benefits only those who already possess significant capital and influence.
